properties.name: Financial District
properties.blurb: The original New Amsterdam — Manhattan south of Wall Street is the oldest part of the city, with streets that follow 17th-century Dutch cow paths rather than the 1811 grid. Wall Street itself is named for the wooden wall built across the island in 1653. The 1916 Equitable Building (still standing on Broadway) cast such a vast shadow that it triggered the country's first comprehensive zoning law.

properties.name: TriBeCa
properties.blurb: Triangle Below Canal — a 19th-century produce-and-textile warehouse district that emptied out by the 1970s. Like SoHo, it was rezoned for residential loft conversions and quickly became one of the most expensive neighborhoods in the city. Robert De Niro launched the Tribeca Film Festival here in 2002 to bring people back after 9/11.

properties.name: Chinatown
properties.blurb: One of the oldest and largest Chinatowns in the West, dating to the 1870s. Its growth was capped by the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act, which is why the neighborhood stayed compact for decades. After 1965 immigration reform it grew dramatically and now extends well into what used to be Little Italy. The street grid here predates the 1811 plan, which is why it feels labyrinthine.

properties.name: Lower East Side
properties.blurb: Once the most densely populated neighborhood on Earth — at its 1900 peak the LES held over 700,000 people in a few square blocks, mostly Eastern European Jewish, Italian, and Irish immigrants. The 1901 New York State Tenement House Act was passed largely in response to LES living conditions.

properties.name: SoHo
properties.blurb: SoHo (South of Houston) was a 19th-century cast-iron warehouse district that nearly became an expressway in the 1960s — until artists and Jane Jacobs–led activists fought it off. The cast-iron facades, originally a cheap mass-produced cladding for textile lofts, are now one of the largest collections of cast-iron architecture in the world.

properties.name: East Village
properties.blurb: For most of the 19th and 20th centuries this was the Lower East Side's northern half — a tenement district packed with German, Eastern European, and later Latino and Ukrainian immigrants. The "East Village" name was coined in the 1960s by realtors trying to attract Beats and bohemians. CBGB on the Bowery birthed punk rock here.

properties.name: West Village
properties.blurb: The grid breaks down here — most of the West Village predates the 1811 Commissioners' Plan that imposed Manhattan's rectangular grid. The result is the city's most walkable, most photographed neighborhood, with crooked streets, low brownstones, and the Stonewall Inn (1969 LGBTQ+ uprising) on Christopher Street.

properties.name: Meatpacking District
properties.blurb: Until the 1990s this was a literal meatpacking district — over 250 slaughterhouses and packing plants in the early 20th century, dwindling to a handful by 2000. Cobblestone streets and loading-dock canopies remain. The transformation into a high-fashion district happened almost overnight after the High Line opened in 2009.

properties.name: Chelsea
properties.blurb: Originally the country estate of Clement Clarke Moore (the man who wrote "A Visit from St. Nicholas") in the early 1800s. Became a working-class district of Irish dockworkers and later a film-industry hub — Chelsea was home to NYC's first movie studios before Hollywood. The High Line elevated rail (1934) shut down in 1980 and reopened as a park in 2009.

properties.name: Hell's Kitchen
properties.blurb: Once one of the most violent neighborhoods in the country — gang-controlled in the 1860s through the mid-20th century, immortalized in West Side Story. The name origin has many versions but is commonly traced to a rookie cop calling a riot scene "hell," with his veteran partner replying "hell's a mild climate. This is hell's kitchen."

properties.name: Midtown
properties.blurb: The world's densest concentration of skyscrapers. Most of what you see was built in two great booms: the 1920s–30s Art Deco era (Empire State, Chrysler, Rockefeller Center) and the post-war International Style (Lever House, Seagram). The 1916 Zoning Resolution is why so many Midtown towers taper as they rise.

properties.name: Times Square
properties.blurb: Originally Longacre Square, a horse-trade district. Renamed in 1904 when The New York Times built its tower here. The first electric advertising signs appeared in 1904; by the 1930s "the Crossroads of the World" was synonymous with NYC nightlife. Crime-and-grime in the 70s–80s was famously cleaned up in the 90s.

properties.name: Upper West Side
properties.blurb: The UWS took off after the 1879 elevated train brought transit to the area. Beaux-Arts apartment palaces — the Dakota, Ansonia, Apthorp, San Remo — clustered along Central Park West and the avenues, attracting artists, intellectuals, and Jewish families. Lincoln Center transformed the southern end in the 1960s.

properties.name: Upper East Side
properties.blurb: The traditional home of "old money" New York. The stretch of Fifth Avenue along Central Park is called Millionaires' Row — the Frick, Carnegie, and Vanderbilt mansions all stood here, several preserved as museums. East of Park Avenue, brownstone blocks like Yorkville historically housed German and Eastern European immigrants.

properties.name: Harlem
properties.blurb: Established as a 17th-century Dutch village (Nieuw Haarlem), Harlem became Manhattan's premier Black cultural center after the 1900s Great Migration. The Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s — Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Duke Ellington at the Cotton Club — made it one of the most influential cultural districts in the world. The 125th Street corridor and Apollo Theater remain its main stage.
